## VIII. Diplomacy (1861)

Hardly a week passed before the newspapers announced that President Lincoln had selected Charles Francis Adams as his Minister to England. Once more, silently, Henry put Blackstone back on its shelf. The Civil Law had lasted a brief day; the Common Law prolonged its shadowy existence for a week. The law, as path of education, vanished in April, 1861, leaving a million young men planted in the mud of a lawless world, to begin a new life without education at all. Mr. Adams intimated that he thought himself entitled to the services of one of his sons, and indicated Henry as the only one who could be spared. Henry packed his trunk again without a word. Ridiculous as he knew himself about to be in his new role, he was at least no public official, no vulture of patronage. The strongest proof of his father's unfitness was perhaps his consent to quit a safe seat in Congress for an exceedingly unsafe seat in London, with no better support than Senator Sumner—at the head of the Foreign Relations Committee—was likely to give him. In the family history, its members had taken many a dangerous risk, but never before had they taken one so desperate.

Minister Adams sailed for England, May 1, 1861, with much the same outfit as Admiral Dupont would have enjoyed if the Government had sent him to attack Port Royal with one cabin-boy in a rowboat. He thought it natural to play the adventurer as his father and grandfather had done before him—John Adams sailing for France in midwinter, John Quincy sailing for Russia to cope with Napoleon and the Czar nearly single-handed. He did not even notice that he left not a friend behind him. This was a lofty view, and for him answered his objects, but it bore hard on cabin-boys. The first time America was posing as the champion of legitimacy and order, and the only rag of legitimacy in the mission was the private secretary, whose stature was not sufficient to impose awe on the Court and Parliament of Great Britain.

The habit of reticence—of talking without meaning—had to begin at once, and it affected him for life. He was already an adept when the party landed at Liverpool, May 13, 1861, and went instantly up to London: a family of early Christian martyrs about to be flung into an arena of lions, under the glad eyes of Tiberius Palmerston. Though Lord Palmerston would have laughed his peculiar Palmerston laugh at figuring as Tiberius, he would have seen only evident resemblance in the Christian martyrs, for he had already arranged the ceremony.

The private secretary thought on May 12 that he was going to a friendly government and people, true to the anti-slavery principles which had been their steadiest profession. He was, like all Bostonians, instinctively English. He supposed himself, as one of the members of a famous anti-slavery family, to be welcome everywhere in the British Islands.

On May 13, he met the official announcement that England recognized the belligerency of the Confederacy. This beginning of a new education tore up by the roots nearly all that was left of Harvard College and Germany. He had to learn—the sooner the better—that his ideas were the reverse of truth; that in May, 1861, no one in England—literally no one—doubted that Jefferson Davis had made or would make a nation, and nearly all were glad of it, though not often saying so. They mostly imitated Palmerston who, according to Mr. Gladstone, "desired the severance as a diminution of a dangerous power, but prudently held his tongue." Lord John Russell, as Foreign Secretary, had received the rebel emissaries and decided to recognize their belligerency before the arrival of Mr. Adams—in order to fix the position of the British Government in advance. The recognition of independence would then become an understood policy: a matter of time and occasion.

Whatever Minister Adams felt, the first effect of this shock upon his son produced only a dullness of comprehension. Yet he realized that to his father it was likely to be fatal. What struck him most, in the long leisure of later reflection, was the cold realization of his situation had his father then shown himself what Sumner thought him to be—unfit for his post. Minister Adams showed no trace of excitement; his manner was the same as ever; not a word escaped; not a nerve twitched. The test was final, for no other shock so violent and sudden could possibly recur. The worst was in full sight. The private secretary knew his own business, which was to imitate his father as closely as possible and hold his tongue.

Socially, under the best of circumstances, a newcomer in London needs years to establish a position. Politically the prospect looked worse still. All of Europe waited to see the Legation go. His duties as private secretary required him to know everybody and go everywhere with his father and mother, yet he had not a friend or even an acquaintance. The solitude was terrible beyond anything he had known.

When the season ended, the private secretary had not yet won a private acquaintance. Bull Run was a worse diplomatic than military disaster. Yet its effect on the Legation was almost strengthening. They no longer felt doubt. For the next year they went on only from week to week, ready to leave England at once, never assuming more than three months for their limit. Europe was waiting to see them go; so certain was the end that no one cared to hurry it.

In December, 1861, Reuter's telegram announced the seizure of Mason and Slidell from a British mail-steamer. All three secretaries, nervous as wild beasts under the long strain—though they knew it to be not merely diplomatic rupture but a declaration of war—broke into shouts of delight. They were glad to face the end. They saw it and cheered it.

They telegraphed the news to the Minister, who was staying with Monckton Milnes at Fryston in Yorkshire. The Trent Affair passed like a snowstorm, leaving the Legation, to its surprise, still in place.

One result of the Trent Affair was personal. Adams had been writing to Henry J. Raymond, and Raymond had used his letters in the New York Times. He had gone down to Manchester to study the cotton famine, and wrote a long account published in the Boston Courier with his name attached—whereupon it was instantly crushed by a long, satirical leader in the London Times. He escaped because he was totally unknown; no one thought twice about it; and the world had other objects of constant ridicule—President Lincoln, Secretary Seward, Commodore Wilkes. Henry Adams escaped, but he never tried to be useful again. "Surtout point de zèle!" Zeal was too hazardous a profession for a Minister's son to pursue among Trent Affairs and rebel cruisers.

Socially, he had but one relief during that first winter. The only gleams of sunshine were days spent at Walton-on-Thames as guest of Mr. and Mrs. Russell Sturgis at Mount Felix. Mrs. Russell Sturgis was one of the women to whom an intelligent boy attaches himself as closely as he can. The kind of education he most required was that of a charming woman, and she could have good-naturedly trained a school of such without an effort. During two years of miserable solitude she was, in that social polar winter, the single source of warmth and light.

Little by little, Minister Adams gained foothold. His extremely quiet manner and unassailable social position did not conciliate British society—they chose to ignore him since they could not ridicule him—but the singular luck that had taken him to Fryston to meet the shock of the Trent Affair under the sympathetic eyes of Monckton Milnes and William E. Forster never afterwards deserted him.

Monckton Milnes was a social power in London, possibly greater than Londoners themselves quite understood, for dull men always laughed at Monckton Milnes—every bore talked familiarly about "Dicky Milnes," the "cool of the evening." Behind his almost Falstaffian mask and laugh of Silenus he carried a fine, broad, and high intelligence which no one questioned. He had written verses, made speeches in Parliament criticised as too good for the place and too high for the audience, and held a social position that ended in a peerage. His breakfasts were famous, and his house in Upper Brook Street was one to which most clever people were exceedingly glad of admission. He was a voracious reader, a strong critic, a collector of books, and above all a man of the world by profession who loved the contacts—perhaps the collisions—of society. Milnes was the good-nature of London; the Gargantuan type of its refinement and coarseness; the most universal figure of May Fair.

Forster was quite the opposite—a tall, rough, ungainly Yorkshireman who had married a daughter of Dr. Arnold and taken up the Union cause with practical energy and honest conviction. Bright and Cobden were the hardest hitters in England, and with all four champions—Milnes, Forster, Bright, Cobden—the Minister could tackle even Lord Palmerston without much fear of foul play.

The old anti-slavery clique proved troublesome, but the Duke of Argyll was one of the most valuable friends the Minister found. The private secretary himself, though he made no effort and silently waited the end, found that through these connections friendliness occasionally reached even him. Whatever might be the advantages of society to his father and mother, to him the whole business of diplomacy was futile. He meant to go home.
